utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning. I would like to greet the parties, the accused, the technical staff, the legal officers, the stenotypists, and the ushers. And I would like to extend my greeting to the public gallery. Would you please let in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning. Before we start, kindly take an oath. We appreciate you very much for coming. Thank you. Now, if you will please take the oath, as he will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Harmon, you are today our Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge Riad. Good morning, Judge Riad, Judge Wald. Good morning colleagues from the Defence, and good morning Captain Rutten.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you state your name please and spell your last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: My name is Captain Rutten, and I could spell my name, it's R-u-t-t-e-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, you're a professional soldier in the Royal Dutch army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you currently hold the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when you and I speak, in the course of my examination, as I've told you before, it's important that you pause after I ask a question so the interpreters can have time to interpret my question and interpret your answer.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you joined the Royal Dutch army in 1981; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you served in DutchBat III in the Srebrenica enclave from January of 1995 until the 21st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, one of your mandates while you were serving in DutchBat was to assist in the delivery of humanitarian aid; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And while you were in the enclave, did aid convoys carrying humanitarian aid in the form of food and medicine arrive in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: They did -- convoys from the UNHCR arrived in the enclave, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there any obstruction of those humanitarian aid convoys?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: They had -- first there was a lot of paperwork with the Serbs before any UNHCR convoy was coming in, and during the whole period in the enclave, we saw decreasing, the number of convoys during the seven months we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And why were the number of convoys carrying humanitarian aid in the form of food and medicine and the like, why did they decrease?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The Serbs wouldn't let in more. The situation in the enclave was, at a certain point, real bad and the Dutch LO team, which means the local negotiators, asked for more assistance from the UNHCR, but the Serbs wouldn't let come in no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what effect, Captain Rutten, did the obstruction of those humanitarian aid convoys have on the population who resided within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Everything that was edible, they tried to get. Even where our garbage was dumped, there was a lot of people when the garbage was really dumped, trying to found something edible in our garbage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there sufficient food for the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 85, which is a photograph, distributed, and if the usher could place a copy of Prosecutor's 85 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the distribution of this exhibit, Captain Rutten, was the obstruction of the aid convoys by the Bosnian Serbs something that you saw on a constant basis or did the obstructions increase as time went on?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It probably increased because we saw less convoys coming in during the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Captain Rutten, there's been a photograph placed on the ELMO. Did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: During patrolling in the enclave, on the route to OP Quebec and Romeo, we saw our garbage truck that we hired local, from the local people there, and they had picked up our garbage there. That was dumped on a mountainside, and these are the local people, the refugees that were inside the enclave of Srebrenica and tried to something edible around the garbage that was dumped in the place where you see on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did this scene repeat itself every time the UN garbage truck went to the dump site?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not the only one that have seen that scene. My colleagues told a lot about it because, yeah, they find it unbelievable that people do that in such a way, as you see here on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, when did the attack on the enclave start? What date?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We had some problems in June, but the real attack on the enclave, from out of the northern side also firing, started on the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. And tell the Judges what occurred on the 10th of July, as you recall it, and what you did.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: On the 10th of July, we heard during the night some impact just behind the compound, real severe impacts. Later it appeared to be fired from a rocket launcher, an M-77 Oganj that was placed in Bratunac. We knew that because later on our local negotiators saw, during the negotiations in Bratunac, that the Oganj, the M-77, was still in place there. And the day after the shelling, at night we found one of the rockets that had not gone off just behind the compound. The days after that, the shelling started more heavier during the day and it stopped during the night, in the late evening. They tried to bind us, more or less, on the compound so we couldn't get off. From out of the hills of Birici, that's near OP Papa, at the entrance of the enclave, they shot more or less in a lane, which is the road that leads from Potocari to Srebrenica, also on our vehicles or nearby, just to intimidate us and to try to stay -- to let us stay at the compound. That evening, on Monday evening exactly, we heard about our other company that was at that moment B Company in Srebrenica, that the situation was growing out of hand and people, the refugees itself from the enclave, were on the move to Potocari. At that point, I got the order to make a hole at the rear side of the compound in the fence so that we could let people in, not by the main entrance but just at the rear side of the compound, if there was a necessity. That evening, some soldiers of the B Company came along with the first refugees, and we kept them at the bus remise because we didn't want to have too much refugees at that time at the compound, at least I haven't got an order at that time to let the people in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Harmon. Captain Rutten just said Monday evening. Was the 10th of July Monday, or was it the 11th?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I started on the 10th, and that's the Sunday, and the 11th is Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That was the 11th. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Captain Rutten, while you were in Srebrenica, what were your normal duties and functions?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: My normal duty was -- I was commander of an anti-tank platoon, but since the means were on the OPs itself and the soldiers also, my second duty was patrol coordinator in the northern area of the enclave and intelligence officer of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, you've described heavy shelling in the Srebrenica enclave. Can you tell me, based on your presence on patrols and your experience in the enclave, were there any military targets in the town of Srebrenica or in the town of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There were no real military targets. The military targets that were there were on the confrontation or border line at that time of the enclave. There were some BiH soldiers still, but not in Potocari or Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is your view on the purpose of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The purpose of the shelling was, at first, to intimidate us not to leave the compound anymore or to see what was really happening outside of the compound, and to, yeah, more or less it was a terror act because the shelling was not on marked goals, you could say, not on marked military goals, you could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to focus your attention on the 11th of July. Tell the Judges what happened.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The 11th of July, as I told you before, it was in the evening, we made a hole in the fence. Eventually no one came in. We sent out a Red Cross APC because they were shelling on the people that had left Srebrenica, on the way to Potocari. They were accompanied by some Dutch -- by a Dutch group of the B Company that had left Srebrenica to accompany them to Potocari. Because of the shelling they had to stay and they came no further than the bus remise. We sent out the Red Cross APC to give assistance over there to the wounded, and that was at that time the stage. I was with a group near the rear side of the compound, at the fence, waiting if there were probably refugees coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, when did the large influx of refugees arrive at the Potocari compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: On Monday evening, finally we closed the fence again, the hole that I made, because no one was coming in. Only a heavily wounded woman we carried over the fence because we had closed the fence then. She was cared for at our battalion hospital, you could say, at Potocari, and brought later in the evening, when she was stabilised, back to Srebrenica again, with a Dutch APC, a Red Cross APC. The next day, and I speak of Tuesday, we were all in a bunker because of the shelling and had to wait. In the morning, I was sent out again because someone was at the main gate and waved with something that looked like a card or a map of the area, and they assumed, the guard assumed, that probably that was a Muslim leader of the Muslim party or whatever. I went out with a colleague, a colleague lieutenant, to see what really was happening. But there were no leaders, there were two soldiers. One was wounded who had a shot through the underarm and was taken care of, before when I saw him, by a Dutch soldier, and I could see that there was a card on his arm and on the card you could see what treatment he had given, the Dutch soldier. We asked him where he came from. He came from the surroundings of OP Mike. And we sent him back to Srebrenica because we couldn't help him. We gave him something to drink and that was the whole of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. Was that a Muslim soldier?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Sorry. That was a Muslim soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: At that time, I went back to the bunker, reported it, what I've seen, to the operations room, and we -- shortly after that we got a new assignment with a group of almost ten men to open the hole in the gate that I made the night before again. I opened it again and we had to wait for what was going to happen. A new group also came out with Lieutenant Koster as leader and had to go to the bus remise to see what was happening over that. At that time, I heard by my communication means that large refugee groups were coming to Potocari, and the B Company had to leave Srebrenica because of the shelling and the total chaos over there. We sent out, from out of the Potocari compound, a lot of trucks so they could assist to get the refugees to the Potocari compound. At that time, the first groups of refugees came by the rear side, sent out by Lieutenant Koster, with his group of men that were, at that time, at the bus remise, sent in at the rear side. That went on almost the whole day, until more or less 5.00, 6.00 in the evening, and more or less 4.000 to 5.000 refugees we held in the compound at that time. At that time also I got the order not to let in more refugees because the factory hall itself was completely filled up with the refugees of the enclave then, and we couldn't have more people over there. There were prepared some meals of the rest of the things we had for the refugees. Still waiting at the fence and had to close it. I got back, and we got with a few colleague lieutenants, from Major Otter, a new assignment to get together three groups of ten men and to secure the refugees during the night that had stayed outside, near the bus remise. We prepared for that, and as it got dark, we went out to secure those refugees that had stayed outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have the usher's assistance, please, and could you place Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/2 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Captain Rutten, you've referred to the bus remise. Would you take a look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/2 and can you identify what you have called the bus remise on Prosecutor's 5/2.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating for the record the Express Bus Compound.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I'm now showing with a pencil where the words say Express Bus Compound. That is that side where I stayed with my group of ten men. In the middle there was another group of Lieutenant Koster's of ten men, and at the Zinc Factory, at the other side, were also a lot of refugees. The group of Lieutenant Schotman also consisted of ten Dutch soldiers with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So for the record, Lieutenant Schotman stayed on the right side of the road that bisects the Prosecutor's 5.2 in the area of the Zinc Factory, and Lieutenant Koster stayed on the left side of the road between the road and the Express Bus Compound on Prosecutor's 5/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you stay there the whole night?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We had the order to stay there the whole night. We saw that there were very many refugees over there. We tried to organise it more or less by -- had red/white tape around the whole area, that everyone could see that that was the area where the refugees were kept by us, because we had no other means to do that, and so making clear to everyone that that was the secure area that was under UN surveillance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the following morning, what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The following morning, in the early morning, there was again some firing on the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "firing," what kind of firing do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Small arms, that was the thing that we heard at first, and later on there was some mortar fire, and we saw some houses burning and some pile of hay that were also on the -- that was harvested by the farmers, was also in flames then. That was to -- I think to make the situation look more worse than it really was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Captain Rutten, let me show you another photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could have Prosecutor Exhibit 5/19 placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, are you familiar with the area depicted in Prosecutor's 5/19?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, it's familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you seen this area on the morning you have just been testifying about?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what you saw in this area?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: When you look at this area, it was all filled up with refugees and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Pointing to the blue buildings.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Pointing to the blue building, yes. It was all filled up around here, almost packed up with refugees. And on the hillside, there were some houses burning. There were harvested crops that day set afire, just to -- and when I mean "they," they were the first Serb soldiers that we saw who came down from the hills. And what kind of types were they? The first one that got to me were more or less the Rambo-types.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain, let me ask you, did you see anything in respect of the houses in the foreground in this Prosecutor's 5/19?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Some of the houses were burning too that were here [indicates], around the bus remise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what effect did these objects that were burning have on the refugees?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The effect was that there was a total panic then because the shooting, the fire, and seeing the Serb soldiers coming in from all sides, the people thought that this was -- something really bad was going to happen. We tried to calm down everything, and as the first soldiers came down, Serb soldiers, I spoke to the first of them that looked to me like a leader. I didn't know if he was one. And I said to him, "You can't go behind the red/white tape because it's UN territory and there are refugees under our surveillance there." He didn't -- not he, but also the rest of the Serb soldiers were just laughing and trying to step over the red/white tape and do as they please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see any of the soldiers threaten any of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We had, during the night, a man in a wheelbarrow came in. I knew the man because he was in the BiH army. Now he was in civilian clothes, wounded at his leg, he had a shot through his leg. The doctor that was with me that night cared for him near the bus remise. The first Serb soldier that was more or less what I just called the Rambo-type made that sign [indicates], a sign along the throat, to the more or less young Muslim soldier that was in the wheelbarrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating, for the record, the sign being a finger running across the throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was your interpretation of that sign?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: My interpretation of that sign, that from that moment on, it was very clear for me that they looked for the man, and it was also very clear to me that the things that were going to happen with the men predicted nothing good.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were you still at the same location near the bus remise?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was still at the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you had your squad of soldiers with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did anything happen to your equipment?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We had between some old buses that were shot and completely torn down, we had to spend the night in shifts, and we had our gear there, our bags, for staying for the night because we didn't know how long we were staying. At that moment, the first Serb soldiers that came in stole a part of the equipment, what they could use, and some personal belongings that were in our equipment. I sent out some soldiers to prevent that, but they were pushed away and sent back to me, and said "Get out of here." At that time that the soldiers were walking back, or tried to walk back, there was some gunfire that came down from the hill, the BiH probably, and then the Serb soldiers fired back using a few of my men as a shield. At that time I walked to the Serb soldiers and said that I had to bring my men back. It was a panic situation, more or less. I grabbed my weapon, I pointed it at the Serbs, and at that time they let go of my personnel so they could get back to me. And then eventually the firing stopped and they went on with the stealing from our gear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, did you make a complaint about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Later, sometime later, I think one hour, I saw our Dutch Captain Matthijsen, which was on the S-5 team, and with him was a Major -- to me known as a Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was Major Nikolic a member of the BSA, the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. I made a complaint to Matthijsen that we were looted by the Serb soldiers and they were threatening the refugees. I also addressed the BSA Major Nikolic, he said that he could do nothing about it but they wouldn't harm the refugees at that time. And he said that it was very difficult for him to get our stuff back. So I made a complaint but I doubted that that was of any use at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me focus your attention on Major Nikolic. Did you know from what unit Major Nikolic came?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: To me, it was known that Major Nikolic was our contact person of the battalion, at least, of the northern part, and in the northern part the Bratunac Brigade was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there another liaison officer from the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There was -- to my knowledge, there was another Bosnian soldier that was also there that was called Jovo at OP Papa. That was the contact, the first contact between OP Papa, the battalion, and the BSA, you could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So if you needed to make a contact with Major Nikolic, for example, you would go to Jovo, who was at OP Papa, and the request would be communicated to Major Nikolic; is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is how it worked, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at some point in time, did something happen to you and your men, that same day?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The time the BSA soldiers came in, we had our vests, we had our weapons, and I had my two communication sets for doing my job over there. During the day I got threatened by the BSA soldiers to give up my weapon, my communication sets, and my vest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when that happened, let me ask you to put it in the context of the time, had buses arrived yet in the enclave, or was this before the arrival of the buses in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The threatening started before the buses arrived, and the real -- the real threat later on was when the buses already were coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the event that you just described occurred as the buses were coming in.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, continue, please, if you would, describing what happened to you and to your men at that time.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: At the point that the buses were coming in, we were threatened, and I at first, had to give up my weapon and my vest and the rest of my things. I sent the men back, because I said, "I don't talk to an NCO," which he probably was, "I need to speak to your commander." And "This is UN gear so I can't give up my gear."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did the same thing that was happening to you happen to your ten men as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. And I ordered them not to give up my -- I ordered them not to give up their weapons or whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they give up their weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Finally they had to because they were threatened with weapons and had to give up their vests and their armoury.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the same thing happen to you? Did you have to give up your weapon and your armour?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. Also the doctor that was standing next to me, someone, a BSA soldier, probably the commander at least, he looked to me like one, came to me and said, "I need your stuff." There was a soldier next to him, grabbing my weapon, and I said, "I can't do that," and I turned away from him, with my back to him. He pulled his gun on my head, at the rear side, and said, "I need your communications set now." I gave him one, and I grabbed my other one and I made my last signal to my superior officer that I lost my weapon now, and that that had been kept now by the Bosnian Serb army. At that time we were taken -- I was at the time at a small bridge in the middle of the bus remise. We were taken to a place next to the bus remise again with the whole group, and we had to stay there, under the surveillance of two Bosnian Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the location where you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: A few hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did that include your other men as well? You and the men?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was including my ten men and the doctor that was with me. At that time I saw someone that looked to me also as an officer, and later on he became known to me as the so-called Captain Mane. I protested with him that we were held there, and I protested to him that we had lost our equipment. He didn't even bother to look at me and sent me back to the rest of the group. Later on when he came back, and I say later on, a few hours later, I protested again and I said that we could do nothing more there and that we had to go back to the compound. And finally he said that we could go back and sent with my group two Bosnian Serb soldiers to escort me to the compound again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 71, please, and could that be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, can you identify the individual on the left-hand side of this Prosecutor's Exhibit 71?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was the so-called Captain Mane.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, did you at some point that day, after your release from captivity, did you see General Mladic in the area of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not the 12th, because the 12th we got back to the compound and we stayed the night over at the compound. But on the 13th, in the afternoon, early afternoon, I saw Mr. Mladic arriving at the compound. And I must correct that. On the 12th, I saw Mr. Mladic for the first time, handing out -- his troops were handing out some bread and water then. That was on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask if I could have the lights dimmed and if I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 78 played, please. The Court has already seen this exhibit, but for purposes of showing this witness and putting his testimony in context, I'm replaying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, that was a very brief snippet of a film that you have seen in my office prior to coming here to testify. Did you see that scene?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was the scene near the road, a house near the road that led from Potocari to Srebrenica. That was the moment on the 12th when Mladic came in, with his bodyguards around him, and there was also a truck behind him and also a firetruck. In the first truck there was bread being distributed among the refugees, and in the firetruck they brought along to give the refugees water they had brought with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, tell the Judges what you saw happen -- actually, let me ask you another question. At the time the candy was being distributed, we've seen the film of at least a portion of that episode, was the distribution of the bread also filmed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Both scenes were filmed, as well as the distributing of the bread, the water, and the handing out of the candy to some children near the house. It was only a short instant that they filmed over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened after the filming stopped?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: After the filming stopped, they stopped also handing out the bread, the water, and the candy. They even took back some of it that they gave to the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At any other time while you were in Potocari on the 12th and the 13th did you see the Bosnian Serbs distribute any other bread, water, food, or anything that would help the refugees?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, they did not. The only thing that got distributed was given by us, and that was some water and the things that we had left for the refugees on the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the image that you just saw on Prosecutor's Exhibit 78 of a soldier, a Bosnian Serb soldier, handing out candy and the scenes that you saw of the distribution of the bread and the water, did that create a correct and accurate impression of the way that the Bosnian Serb soldiers in the enclave were treating the refugees?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, not really, because it was a short moment that they showed some, you could say, mercy to the refugees, but it stopped at the moment the cameras went away. And from that moment on, they started filling up the buses that had also arrived then, and behind the buses, there you directly saw that the men were separated from the rest of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, what's your impression of the purpose of that filming of those generous moments?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: To me it looked more or less like a media campaign or propaganda, whichever word you want to use, because it stopped after a very short time. It looked like, to the world and to us at first, that they were showing, as I told you, some mercy to the refugees, but in fact it was all a big play and well registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Captain Rutten, did you have access to Dutch national television in your compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was that through a satellite transmission?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We had a satellite transmission, but the days that we had to cope with the refugees and when we had to do our task, we couldn't see any of it. But two days later, on Friday, we saw the Dutch news on our TVs, and we saw the same scenes, on which we saw one of them here right now, Mladic with his soldiers handing out candy, bread, and that was what the world saw two days later. We were completely astonished then in our room where we had our TV because, yeah, we couldn't understand that those films were that fast shown to the whole world.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And at the time you saw those films, were there any refugees left in and around the compound at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There were none left then, the moment we saw it. It was Friday then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/4, please, and if that could be placed on the ELMO. Before we put that on the ELMO, Captain, did I show you the exhibit that the usher is holding in his hand, this binder with a number of individuals in it, and did you identify somebody in that binder?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you place Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/4 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, do you recognise anyone in this particular image?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise that man [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating, for the record, the second individual from the right-hand side of the image, the man in the foreground with an orange face.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did you see that individual?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I saw him in one of the cars that accompanied Mr. Mladic near the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me change the topic and ask you, Captain Rutten, are you familiar with a location known as the White House?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you go to the White House?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you first go to the White House? What date?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: First I went to the White House on the Thursday, Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/17 and then 83 given to the usher. Mr. Usher, if you could place Prosecutor's 5/17 on the ELMO, and if the assistant could disseminate Prosecutor's Exhibit 83 to the Judges and to counsel before I show it. Could you place Prosecutor's 5/17 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recognise that particular building, Captain Rutten?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was what we all called the White House.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Usher, if you could place Prosecutor's Exhibit 83 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Captain Rutten, this is a picture that you took; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you identify the location of the front gate of the UN compound and the location of the White House?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This is the entrance of the compound [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Keep your pointer there for just a moment so I can describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating, for the record, in about the middle of the picture, near the road, there appears to be a road that travels from the middle of the picture diagonally to the left, and there is a bunker facility that has a blue flag atop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that's the entrance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could you move your pointer to the location of the White House?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This is the White House [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating a building with a rusted roof on, looks like, a flat field or a flatter area below the hill, and it's to the left of the entrance to the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Captain Rutten. So the White House really wasn't far from the entrance to the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. We could see it when we were at the entrance and the guard could see it almost constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you go to the White House?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That morning I had a duty at the operations room, and we heard that -- by transmission, that a colleague had seen two buses leave, and the colleague was a Lieutenant Versteeg who saw two buses leave nearby the White House, filled up with men. We had outside several jeeps in place to accompany or to escort the buses when they left the enclave. This lieutenant saw the two buses leave and asked to our ops room if he had to escort those two buses. I ordered him to immediately follow those two buses because they were separately leaving and not leaving with the greater amount of buses that were also ready along the road. At that time he accompanied the buses to Bratunac, and the next transmission we got was the bus is going not on the way to Kladanj, but turns another way, "and I am being obstructed now by Bosnian Serb soldiers to follow the bus." I said to him, "Try to stay with the bus," but it wasn't possible at all because the Bosnian Serbs blocked his car and even hijacked his car, more or less. And he and his driver were later on brought back to the compound. So we never knew where those two buses went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So based on that series of events, did you decide to go to the White House personally?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I spoke to my company commander and I said, "Perhaps it's good to have a look outside, at what's really happening, because if we get everything through transmission, we might not be getting a clear picture." So I went outside, accompanied by a sergeant major. We took with us a wheelbarrow with water, filled up with packages of water, and went to the White House to have a reason to be there, and tried to get into the White House. As we came at the gate, we saw that, on the left side of the entrance, where the pointer is now, a great, a huge pile of rucksacks and another belongings of the refugees. A few metres further on, on the ground there were all kinds of identity cards, passports. And then you get to the house, and that was guarded, well guarded by Bosnian Serb soldiers. We tried to get in at first but they wouldn't let us. There were also, in front of the house, two Dutch soldiers that had been given stars on their soldiers, that were in effect corporals. Why they got stars, it looked better to the Bosnian Serbs that there is a lieutenant around than if there is just a mere soldier around. We tried to inspect the house but we didn't come in at first. We walked around the house. We got in at the rear side, and I can point it out to you. This is the rear side of the house [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating, for the record, it appears the pointer is on the left-hand side of the house.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We went in, and that means the sergeant major and I. We had a look around, downstairs and on the first floor, and everywhere, in every room we came, we found on the ground, on the couches, and on the bed, all kinds of photographs laying next to each other. It looked to me whether they were looking for something or some familiar faces or something, and, yeah, the whole house was -- yeah, it looked like if there was just a burglary. And, okay, we couldn't find nothing there. In that part of the house, there was no one around. So we tried to go around the house. I saw behind the house, and that's here [indicates], behind the electricity pole, some -- sitting on two chairs, Serb soldiers, two of them. I went to them. They sat in front of a little orchard. I asked them whether I could go further, to have a look around. They wouldn't let me. And if I persisted to go on, one of them pointed a weapon at me and said, "Get the hell out of here," so I had to leave. Coming at the entrance again, or I went back to the house and I heard some voices at the rear side of the house, inside of the house. I couldn't see through the window because it was blinded, more or less. I said to the sergeant major, we tried to get in again. We went to the wheelbarrow, we offered the Serb soldiers some water, and that was the moment we could get in. When we came in the corridor, there was a Muslim man hanging at the staircase with one arm. I asked the Bosnian Serb soldier to lower him so he could reach his two feet to the ground, so he would be more comfortable, and at that time, when I was asking that, I went to the right side of the corridor and that was the room that -- where I heard the voices before, and it looked to me as an interrogation room and I tried to get in. But at that moment, the Bosnian Serb soldier put a weapon in my face and eventually he stuck it in my mouth, so it -- I had to leave, so I had to pull back more or less. At that time it was very clear to me that there was something going on, and I tried to get a better picture of it. We got some new water, and I told the sergeant major that he had to stay on the staircase and that I would go upstairs to have a look. At that moment, as we stepped outside, we saw at the entrance new men coming in. The soldier at the gate, the Serb soldier at the gate, said "Throw down your things," made just an arm gesture, and a few metres further on, they had to throw their identity cards. At that moment I went in again, went upstairs. The sergeant major stayed at the staircase. As I came up to the first floor, there were two rooms. They were filled up with, more or less, 50 men, and by "men," I mean men from 45 to 55, and some children, some 12 to 13 years old, all boys. I made one arm gesture, upstairs in both rooms, meaning that they have to sit next to each other so that I could make a photograph. I had a camera with me. I made a picture, several pictures, in both rooms, to have a picture of them and, yeah, to testify, to clear, or whatever it later may be good for, that those men were in that house on that day. I had to stop because new men came in, and a Serb soldier came up. So I put away my camera and went down again, and we left the house. It was clear to me that the moment we left the house, that this was no normal interrogation, as we normally teach our own soldiers, because we let the ID and the belongings of the soldiers, when we take someone into custody, or a prisoner of war, in an envelope, and we more or less mark the person that goes with the envelope; otherwise, you cannot clear or state later what person belongs to the belongings or to the IDs. So it was to me very clear that they wouldn't be needing it anymore, the IDs and their belongings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, did you eventually see what happened to those belongings that were in front of the White House?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: In the late evening, on Thursday, and in the early morning, they set all the stuff that was outside, the belongings and the IDs, afire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 84, please, placed on the ELMO. Your Honours have already seen a previous exhibit of these items in front of the White House set on fire, but let me introduce another exhibit, a similar exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, what is this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This is a photograph that I made, standing on a table, looking over our prefabs that you see in front of the photograph, here [indicates], and what you see is here is the entrance of the gate and here [indicates], what is burning, is in front of the White House, and that is the White House.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Right. The smoke.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: You see the smoke of the burning of the belongings and of the IDs of the men that came into the house, of the Muslim men that came into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long do you recall that fire burning?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It burned almost for two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me just clarify just a couple parts of your testimony about your visit to the White House. You said in your testimony that when you first went to the White House, you went to the left-hand side of it, to the rear, and you entered an area that was apparently vacant, there was nobody in it. Was this White House divided into two portions?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that it was a -- that there were actually two houses under one roof, two separate houses under one roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned, Captain Rutten, that you saw a number of photographs laid out. Were these photographs laid out in an orderly fashion, or did it appear that they were thrown about at random?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. They were laying down in an orderly fashion, and the ones that were laying next to each other were all men and not women.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who did you think had laid out those photographs?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I think that it was the men, the Bosnian Serb men that were around there and in the other side of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you one point of clarification. You said at one point you tried to enter an interrogation room, and a weapon was placed near your face. Could you describe the man who did that? What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: He was a Bosnian Serb soldier. He was wearing a green camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, after you left the White House, Captain Rutten, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: After we went -- after that we went to the blockade of four APCs. There I spoke to a local interpreter of ours, a Muslim who lived in the enclave. Admir was his name. And he said that there were rumours from the refugees that there were men killed near a well, near the road, on the Budak side. I asked my colleague, who was in charge there, and that was Lieutenant Koster, that it seemed to me that we had a look over there because under our eyes, more or less, was happening something that we hadn't heard earlier about it or, yeah, we hadn't seen. So I went together with Lieutenant Koster and Sergeant Major van Schaik through the blockade, through the APC blockade, that consisted of four APCs where the Lieutenant van Duijn was around, the Dutch Lieutenant van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain, let me interrupt you there for just a moment. It will be perhaps easier for you to illustrate with the Prosecutor's next exhibit where you went. And if I can have Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/3C placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you could use this exhibit, Captain Rutten, to illustrate where you started, where the blockade was, and where you went.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: On this image you see that the blockade was here [indicates] and here were the four APCs --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating where the yellow line starts, at the other end of the yellow line is an oval shape with the word "bodies".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Then the three of us went up to where the yellow line starts, go to the right, up along the road. It is a dirt road. Here [indicates] we saw a man running from one of these houses, running down. I tried to speak to him but he ran just away. Further up I saw a woman. I asked her if she heard something about any men or whatever, or a well. I know a few words that I learned during patrolling. She marked at me and pointed further up the road, and what she marked was that there were some killings. She also made that sign along her throat [indicates], that there were some killings up that road. So we went up the road. It's a real bushed area. We saw here [indicates] a small stream at the left side, just behind the house, and there is a meadow. And the moment we saw the meadow, we saw also, along the stream, some men lying there. As we got into the meadow, we saw that the men were shot down. I inspected all the men that were on the ground. They were all civilian men, at least they had civilian clothes on. There were nine of them. They were laying with their faces towards the stream. Two were laying on their sides, as if they had looked back. The rest of them were laying with their faces to the stream. They all had shots at their back, at heart height. They were shots of small calibre weapons. The men were all about 45 to 55 years old. The blood was still running. There were no flies on them. It was very warm that day. So you could easily say that it hadn't been long ago that they were shot. At that moment I said to the sergeant major to pick up the ID that was on the grass in the meadow, in front of the refugees, and I made a photo, one photo, with my colleague, with Lieutenant Koster, sitting on his knees between the dead men, and I made a photo as a whole of the nine men that were laying along the stream. At that moment there was some firing at us, so we couldn't stay any longer there. The moment the firing started, first a shot, I saw a woman running out of the houses that are here [indicates] between the bushes, and she was chased by a Bosnian Serb soldier. At that moment I said to the sergeant major, "Okay. Drop all the ID that you've got in your -- that you picked up, and we have to leave here now." Lieutenant Koster said there was another shot -- we heard something and he said, "The shots are nearby. We have to leave." And at that moment we went again up the dirt -- down the dirt road, to more or less the street from Potocari to Srebrenica. And we tried to get back. At the blockade we grabbed a stretcher, more or less so it looked like we were helping some refugees, and got back to the blockade, to the Dutch side. Some time later, and I think five or ten minutes later, I spoke to the Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, that I found nine bodies and that I made a picture of them. And I said, "It is very clear now that they do shoot the men that are around," the Muslim men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, let me just make a number of clarifications on your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the purposes of the record, in Captain Rutten's testimony, he indicated that on his way up, and before he found the bodies, he saw a man running from the house, and for purposes of the record, Captain Rutten pointed to a number of houses, three houses above the yellow dotted line that are in the centre of the picture, and it was from that location that he said he saw the man running from the houses. Also, when he said the woman near the well who he had talked to who had indicated a direction to travel, it indicated a sign again, the sign that was used by Captain Rutten was a finger going across the throat. When Captain Rutten testified that he saw a woman running out of a house near the trees, he was referring to a location that was in the trees, slightly to the left of the oval shape and before one gets out onto the clear road that leads to the main road to Bratunac and Potocari. I wanted to clarify the record for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a couple of other questions in respect of your observations. You personally went down and touched these bodies, didn't you, Captain Rutten?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were the bodies cold? Were they warm?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, they were warm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were there any boys amongst the nine bodies that you saw?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, there were no boys around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were any of the bodies that you saw wounded in the head?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, none. All had back shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me place on the ELMO Prosecutor's Exhibit 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, this was in the area with which you were familiar, because this was an area where you had done your patrols; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm very familiar with the terrain over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that other colleagues of yours had also found bodies in that same area?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. And one of those colleagues was named "Oosterveen"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was the Warrant Officer Oosterveen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The diagram that is in Prosecutor's 82 is a diagram that you prepared. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you show the Court using your pointer the road that you took, that was indicated on the previous exhibit, in the general area where you found the bodies that you found, using your pointer.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay. This is the road that I used [indicates], and I went up here. This is the meadow that I talked about [indicates], and here are nine little lines, indicating the nine bodies I found.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, there's a rectangle at the top of the diagram, and there are nine parallel lines, and it is the area that Captain Rutten was just referring to. And the road that Captain Rutten took on Prosecutor's 82 is the road that is seen starting on the right-hand side of that rectangle and going directly down, intersecting with a road that leads from the right to the left of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Captain Rutten, was it Lieutenant Oosterveen who discovered the other bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, it was a NCO, a warrant officer, a senior warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Senior Warrant Oosterveen. Show the Court the route that senior officer Oosterveen took in the location where he found the bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Oosterveen went up here, and that is also a small stream, at least when it had rained, there was a small stream here, and he went up here [indicates] and that's where he made his photograph, he said to me. Oosterveen was a staff NCO, so he was not as much outside as we were. And our bodies, as I call them like that, that I indicated on the meadow, is along a stream that flows from the north to south, and there was a water wheel just behind the house. Here is also a stream, but that stream was also -- only filled with water during heavy rainfall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this question, Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, by the way, the path indicated by Captain Rutten on Prosecutor's 82 is a -- starts to descend below the words "pad Oosterveen" and the line and the route of Warrant Officer Oosterveen again intersects with the same main road in the -- going from the right to the left-hand side of the diagram. Now, could I have Prosecutor's 82 -- I'm sorry, 5/3A placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, do you think 11.00 would be a suitable time for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a diagram, Mr. President and Your Honours, that was introduced through Witness F.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see the oval-shaped area in -- the upper oval-shaped area in Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/3A?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that area. Now, is that area the same area or a different location where you found your bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: To me, when you look at the map, it is a different area because in the drawing that you saw just before, you can easily see that this is the path that I'd drawn there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That was Oosterveen's path.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was Oosterveen's path. And I went up here [indicates], where you see the APCs, I went up here and went right at this larger road, went up higher here [indicates], to the meadow that is here just behind the house. And here is the house with -- that house. Just behind that house there was a small stream with a waterwheel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, do you therefore conclude that the bodies that you saw were different than the bodies that were seen by Warrant Officer Oosterveen.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think this is an appropriate time to conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll be back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, before the break we were -- I was asking you questions about the discovery of certain bodies, and you had testified that when you returned from the discovery of those bodies, you went, took a stretcher, and returned to the compound, I believe. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, we didn't go directly to the compound. At first I saw, a few minutes later, the Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans. I spoke to him and I said that I'd found nine bodies in the meadow and that I made some pictures of it. He said that he would give the report to a higher level. And from that moment on, we didn't go directly back to the compound. We stayed around with the blocking, with the blockade, where the APCs are. There I tried to make some pictures behind the APCs, showing what the Serbs were doing and more or less also what we were doing. Looking through the camera I saw a picture that didn't look that good, because one of our lieutenants and our men were actually assisting the deportation of the Muslims, trying to do their best to help the refugees. But looking through the camera, as I said, it wouldn't give too good an idea of what the UN was doing over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Captain Rutten, the pictures that you took in the White House, the pictures that you took of the bodies, were those pictures developed, or did something happen to those pictures in the development process and therefore they were never developed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I kept the film with me, until I got back in Holland again, after the 21st of July, 1995. Two days later, a day later, in fact, the 23rd, someone of the intelligence branch of the army came to me and picked up the film, and I gave it to him with the idea that it got developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In fact, you were informed later that that film, something had happened to it during the development process; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me focus your attention back, then, to the next set of events in which you were engaged, and that is the request to escort buses. Could you tell the Judges, did you receive that order and what did you do in response to it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: During the day I got an order to -- from my company commander to escort the last buses that were leaving the enclave. We prepared for it, my driver and I, to get some gear and a jeep, and prepared and placed the jeep next to the entrance to wait until the last refugees had gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say you placed your vehicles next to the entrance, you mean the entrance to the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the entrance to the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while you were waiting to escort buses, did you have an occasion to return to the White House?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: As we waited for the last buses to leave, I told my driver, "It's good to let you see what is happening in the White House," to get as many witnesses as possible of the things that were happening over there. He went with me. We walked around the house. At that time there was at the entrance a huge pack of belongings of the refugees. Also many more IDs and passports were laying on the ground. We went to the side that was empty that morning, that same morning. That side there were two Bosnian Serb soldiers on the staircase. On the staircase itself was filled up with Muslim men. The moment I came around the corner of the house, they looked at me and they had a weapon on the Muslims and the Muslims were handing out to the Bosnian Serb soldiers Deutschemarks, which they had with them at that time. They stopped at the moment that I came, and I walked around the house. In front of the house, there was a balcony that was totally filled up with refugees, all men, and boys in fact. We went to the other side of the house. We couldn't get in then. There were more Bosnian Serb soldiers around, and I think that at that moment almost 300 men were in the house itself and on the balcony. It was completely filled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the condition of those men?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: As we were to the place that I told you before, near the staircase, you could see the total fear, and I never thought that it really existed, but you could even smell death there because it was total fear, what you saw on the faces of the men and the young boys. And that was the thing that I wanted to show to my driver too. Then we went around to have a quick look, and seeing that so many refugees were in the house, we said to each other, "They have to go out here. It's no way to stay here." And I talked to the two Dutch soldiers that were still in place in front of the White House, and they said too, "The house is completely filled up." Then we went back to the entrance and I spoke to some -- one is a Dutch major and a Warrant Officer Rave that was also of the battalion, and we said "Why can't the men go from the house? Because we have to do something at least to get them out of the house," because there was no way they could stay there. "You have to speak to the Bosnian Serbs over there and see whether you could get them into a bus or whatever, because staying there is no use for them." Finally Rave and Major Kingori went to the White House and spoke to the Bosnian Serbs, and some time later, a bus came to get some of the men out, and later on more buses came to get them out again. And they also drove away and we couldn't escort them because we had to wait until the last buses -- yeah, we had to escort the last buses out, so we had to wait. And no one else could escort them because all of the jeeps and soldiers that were escorting the convoys of buses were either thrown out of the buses or pushed out, and the jeeps were hijacked by the Bosnian Serbs. So if we continued the process of escorting the buses, we had no jeeps left. So more or less it was no use to escort them when you lose all your materiel and are brought back half an hour back to the compound, or a day later. And, yeah, the escort hadn't succeeded at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, Captain Rutten, when you said you came around the corner of the White House and you saw Bosnian Serb soldiers relieving Muslims of their Deutschemarks, how were those soldiers dressed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Those were soldiers dressed in the green camouflage uniform of the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/8.1 placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You've seen this photograph before, Captain Rutten. Let me ask you to -- as soon as it's placed on the ELMO. Let me ask you, during your second visit when you were at the White House, did you see a man who you see in Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/8.1 at the White House?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was this man I saw at the White House [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating, for the record, the man in the brown T-shirt on the left-hand side of Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/8.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what did you observe him doing?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: He was talking to the soldiers of the Bosnian Serb army. To me he looked not like a plain soldier, because he spoke to everyone who was around. He spoke not only to the Bosnian Serb soldiers but all men of the Bosnian Serbs that came in front of the house, and I mean also private cars that came along containing also some soldiers but in different uniforms, and by "different uniforms," I mean black uniforms, and spoke to them. Some of the cars were coming out of Srebrenica itself and stopped in front of the White House, he spoke with, and some of them came out of the direction of Potocari, stopped in front of the White House, spoke to each other, spoke to the man here on the photograph, and then leave again with the car, again to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see the men in the black uniforms go into the White House?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, they didn't go into the White House.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Describe the people, the soldiers, and how they were dressed, specifically the ones who went into the White House and who were in and around the White House.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The ones who were in and around the White House were all soldiers, the Bosnian Serb army, wearing green camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at some point in time -- let me ask you this question: How long did you observe the man who was in Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/8.1 at the White House?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Well, sometime it's difficult to say, but he spoke somewhere between 15 to 20 minutes, he was around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At some point in time, Captain Rutten, did you leave the area of the White House and did you start your escort duties?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, later on, when it was clear that the last buses were filled up. The first bus started driving. At that time the battalion had said -- we stopped escorting because it was no use anymore. I asked at my company ops room whether I could go and escort the last to make an attempt to escort the last buses. I got an okay and I drove quickly to the head of the convoy. The first buses were driving. As we got in front of the convoy, we saw in our back mirror, at least the driver saw it at first, that a car, a private car, had come behind us and in the car were three Bosnian Serb soldiers. I instructed my driver, I did it before but I did it again in the car, "The moment we get blocked or whatever or they try to hijack us or whatever, turn the car and drive back because it's no use then to escort the bus or to have an attempt to escort the bus."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, how far had you travelled -- first of all, did you travel in the direction of Bratunac with those buses?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't reach Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you travelling, however, in the direction of Bratunac, from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I was travelling in the direction -- and also in the direction of the entrance of the enclave, more or less, and that was with OP Papa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did this private car come from?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: One of the small dirt roads between the meadows, along the street, the car drove up, the one behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you identify or can you describe the people who were in it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: They were all Bosnian Serb soldiers, wearing also the green camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: What next happened was that another car came also from the side of the road and blocked our road. There were two soldiers in it. So we couldn't go much further. And they pointed at us with weapons. At that moment, I gave my driver the sign to make a u-turn and to go back. We hovered more or less along the road, along the side of the road, and got back along the buses that were driving up to OP Papa, and we went back because it was no use getting your car hijacked and not getting your mission completed, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the soldiers in the vehicle that blocked your escort vehicle from the front?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Those were also Bosnian Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, as a result of making that u-turn, was there any escort for that bus convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, there wasn't any escort left at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to that particular convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure. It went on the route to Kladanj, but I didn't know if it ever reached it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How far away from Potocari was it that this series of events that you've just described took place?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: About a kilometre, a kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Had you reached the location of OP Papa yet?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, did it appear to you that what was happening to you was organised?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I think that it was well organised, because having no one on the buses, having no UN car around, it was impossible for us to secure the road to Kladanj and impossible for us to see what happened to the refugees which were on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I take it you returned to the UN compound after that.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I returned. And the moment I came to the entrance, the major of the staff guard told me that I had to go with a truck and some medical personnel, to go into Srebrenica and to pick up the last elderly people that were left behind or along the road, or whatever, and to get them also on the remaining buses and trucks that were standing along the road, waiting for the last few refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you follow that order?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I followed the order and I went in with the truck, on the road to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were you driving?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I was driving a Mercedes jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: In a turn, at first I saw on a hill some soldiers. We stopped. There were two soldiers next to the road. I spoke to them. They were BiH soldiers. They had no weapons on them, but certainly they were in the house that was on the hill, where the rest of the soldiers were. I think there were at least ten men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were these men that you had become acquainted with on your patrols?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I saw some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: And I stepped out of the car, spoke to them. I said, "It's not good to go to either Srebrenica," and they shouldn't go to Potocari, because it's an enormous risk to go to Potocari. I said, "It would be better to leave the enclave, and the most possible road then is the Bulijen [phoen] area, which is a very wooded area, so you have a real chance to reach the Muslim territory." Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Then we got in the car again. First I grabbed out of the car a few food parcels. I gave them the few food parcels we had left because I -- yeah, it's quite a long distance out of the enclave, through the Bulijen area, to Kladanj itself, so they had to travel for a while. Then we went on, and a few hundred metres further on the road, in a bend, I got stopped by the Bosnian Serb army soldiers again, and they pointed at me with weapons. It all got very hasty. They pulled out the driver and they also said that I had to step out. The sergeant that was in the back of the jeep made the last communication message and turned on the switch to another channel, and that was it, because they hijacked our jeep and we -- they said that we had to go further on the road and complete our mission, or whatever we were doing with the truck. I had to explain that we were going to pick up some elderly people, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you continue on in the direction of Srebrenica in the truck?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, we went on to Srebrenica with the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see anything unusual as you were driving in the direction of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was a total mess along the road. But along the football field, I saw next to the hill, and that's quite a distance, I saw some Bosnian Serb soldiers in camouflage uniforms and some civilian people. But there were also some Bosnian Serb soldiers along the road, and they gave me the sign to drive through and not to stop over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you eventually arrive at UN Bravo Company base?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. We got stopped on the road several times. They all were men that were asking for all kinds of things from us, and finally we reached the Bravo compound. It was more or less destroyed as a compound itself. The fences were down. There were all Bosnian Serb soldiers looting and stealing the compound of the UN possessions that were around there and Dutch possessions that were around there. They were even driving in Dutch APCs. They were totally filled up with everything that they had stolen. They cleared out the weapon collection point where the materiel was of the BiH that was in the enclave. They drove with a T-54 or 55 tank that they also had picked up out of the weapon collection point on the B Company compound. I spoke to a Bosnian Serb soldier. He looked to me like someone that has any rank whatsoever. I asked him if there were men or women around, Muslim people that were sick or whatever, that I could pick up. They said, "There's one man," and he escorted me on the compound. And as we reached the place where the men could have lain, you could see that they could have had someone laying on a ground. There was a blanket but that was it. There was no man around anymore. So we left. The moment we left, there was also a Bosnian Serb in a black uniform and said, "In the houses are much more people.
