You have to pick up that people." You know, "We don't go into houses. We just pick up the people that are outside." We found a few people along the road to Srebrenica, elderly people. The medical personnel treated them and laid them in the truck. Some were very old, and they wouldn't leave the enclave anymore because it's no use for them, they said, to leave the enclave. As we drove around in Srebrenica, we saw two dead bodies in the streets. They were completely swollen, probably from the warmth. They were shot earlier, I think. We couldn't stop at all places. At some places I did stop. In front of the great bazaar or supermarket that was in Srebrenica there were some Bosnian Serb men. I spoke to them and they told me, "Don't worry. In a week you'll be in Holland again and you'll forget all about this."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain Rutten.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've concluded my direct examination of Captain Rutten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Captain Rutten, you will now be questioned by the Defence counsel, and I give the floor -- which one of you both will deal with our witness? Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, you said, during your examination-in-chief, that you recognised the individual shown on a photograph, Exhibit 28/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please place the photograph on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where and when did you see that individual?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the man, he was accompanying Mr. Mladic when he was in front of the compound, on Thursday, the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Captain Rutten, have you ever seen before General Krstic, who is in the courtroom with us today?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I have seen him before but not when I was in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I ask you my next question, I should like to tell the Chamber that Mr. Harmon has informed me that the report on Srebrenica, that is, the report on the debriefing of Srebrenica, is a public document, and I shall, therefore, take the liberty of using it in my cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to raise that issue at the conclusion of the examination, but Defence Exhibit D1 was the exhibit that was tendered by the Defence, and the acceptance of that as a public document was deferred until I could ascertain whether, in fact, it was a public document. I can tell the Chamber now that it is a public document, and we have no objection to Defence Exhibit D1 being removed from the protection of the seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Then you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, from that document, from the same report, I should like to use several fragments during my cross-examination, and I should like to ask the usher to help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He will.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Much to our regret, we have the translation only into Serbo-Croatian. But I gave the interpreters the document in the advance, so that I hope there will be no difficulties in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Captain, while you were on duty in the enclave between January and June 1995, did you ever assess the respective strength of the Bosnian Muslim forces and the Bosnian Serb forces who surrounded the enclave at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I was aware that there was one Bosnian Serb brigade in the north, the Bratunac Brigade, and one --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell me yes or no now. Answer with yes or no, and then later on we may belabour this point further. So did you make such an assessment of the Bosnian Muslim forces and Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, we made some assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I shall read to you passage 2.34 of the report on the debriefing, and I shall then invite you to comment on it. "The ABiH forces in the enclave were divided into four brigades with the overall strength of 3.000 to 4.000 men. Their armament comprised almost exclusively light weapons, complemented with inter alia a limited number of heavy machine-guns, anti-tank armourment, and mortars. Although the DutchBat, in compliance with this mission, did all in its power to disarm the ABiH, the battalion succeeded in this only in part. Regular ABiH troops were reinforced by the local police. Their operations were fairly unpredictable because those units had received practically no training and were rather undisciplined. The ABiH forces conducted systematic actions from the enclave, and after that, they would withdraw into the territory protected by the United Nations." Captain Rutten, is this correct, what the passage in the report says, passage 2.34?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It's partly correct because there were that amount of soldiers probably, but you couldn't call them real soldiers because they were refugees, more or less, placed in duty by a man called -- as you speak of the ABiH soldiers, placed in a sort of a brigade system by Mr. Oric. And you can't speak really of any army, real army structure, but more or less about a permanent group of a few hundred men and the rest were all more or less people, refugees, that were ordered into the army, ABiH army, as you could call it like that, by Mr. Oric, more or less forced. The estimation -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The estimation of the Bosnian Serbs was difficult for us to make because we couldn't see at the other side of the boundary of the enclave --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, I will come to that later on. I'm sorry for interrupting you, but I should like us to keep, for the moment, this subject in mind, that is, your assessment of the strength of the Muslim forces. The last sentence in this passage of the report of the Ministry of Defence says: "The forces of the army of BH conducted systematic actions from the enclave, after which they would withdraw into the territory protected by the United Nations." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I can't say whether that was true or not. We weren't aware of it. We heard some of the stories by the earlier called Major Nikolic, told by our local negotiation team. But we ourselves haven't checked any such information that the ABiH army was having raids outside of the enclave. For us, the ABiH was partly disarmed and the armament was in the weapon collection point, and partly we didn't succeed in disarming the BiH. But what I have seen of the BiH was that they only had small armaments partly and light mortars -- that was the only thing I've ever seen by the BiH -- and some RPGs, that is, an anti-tank weapon, and that's it. And they had almost no ammunition. Because I spoke to several BiH leaders of the northern part, and I was regularly on patrol, and I never, during my whole period, saw a large amount of ammunition or weapons of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should now like to move on to another area, another passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the usher please help.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The passage is 2.35, from the same document, that is, the official report of the Dutch Ministry of Defence, based on the debriefing in Srebrenica. Passage 2.35 addresses the strength of the Bosnian Serb forces and says: "The army of the Republika Srpska had until and ending with June had between three and four battalions belonging to three brigades of the Drina Corps deployed around the enclave. The average strength of the battalion was 250 men. The units were well-equipped and had tanks, armoured caterpillar vehicles, artillery, and mortars. Men in the units were mostly made of Bosnian Serb refugees who had lived in the enclave before. One cannot exclude the possibility that the regular units of the VRS had been reinforced by radical police. The area along the southern boundary of the enclave was not occupied by the VRS, and it was manned instead by combat patrols. The only road in that area was blocked by mines. The VRS used infantry, several offensives of lesser importance because of the structural shortage of manpower. The strength of the VRS was in the use of heavy weaponry. The operations conducted by VRS forces were adjusted to the maintenance of the status quo and of the protection of the Bosnian Serb population in the enclave against the army of BH, carried out, launched, from the enclave."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge Riad, may I -- I have a copy of the English translation of this, and if counsel is going to ask the witness questions about this particular exhibit that's in B/C/S, may I provide to the witness the English translation of that so he may refer to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I believe that that would be very appropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And then if it can be returned to me, I can later file a copy or give a copy of the English translation to counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You will have to see to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon, for the assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, is it correct what this report of the Dutch Ministry of Defence says, in passage 2.35? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can you read this passage to us, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: You mean passage 235?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: "Happening up to and including June, the BSA had between three and four battalions belonging to three brigades of the Drina Corps positioned around the enclave. The average strength of the battalions was 250 men. The units were well-equipped and had tanks, tracked armoured vehicles, artillery, and mortars. The units were manned chiefly by Bosnian Serb refugees who had formerly lived in the enclave. It should not be precluded that the regular BSA units were reinforced by radical militia. The area along the southern boundary of the enclave was not occupied by the BSA but was guarded by means of combat patrol. The through-road in the area was sealed off by mines. A structural shortage of infantry men meant that the BSA launched what amounted to minor offensive on foot. The BSA strength lay in use of the heavy weapons. Operations by the BSA troops around the enclave were geared to maintaining the status quo and protecting the Bosnian Serb population in the enclave from offences by BiH from within the enclave." Reading it again, the things that I have saw myself, in regard to the report, is that it is right that there are -- there were some Bosnian Serb people that lived around the enclave and in the enclave itself, formerly, that we saw on the hills and around the enclave. But by the end of June, we saw, from the OPs, regularly movement of regular BSA army; and then I mean well-equipped soldiers as meant in the report, and not poorly equipped. And there were more infantry men than we saw here in this report. And we saw, at the end of the month of June, more tanks and more artillery placed on the hills around the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In other words, Captain Rutten, the Serb forces began to receive reinforcements sometime in June, in early June, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was what we noticed. By the beginning of June to the end of June, we saw a build-up of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, if you could, will you please comment on the last sentence in this passage, 2.35? I mean, operations conducted by the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska, right up to the eve of the attack on the enclave. The sentence is: "The operations conducted by VRS forces were adjusted to maintaining the status quo and protecting the Bosnian Serb population in the enclave against the offensives of the Army of BH launched from within the enclave." Could you tell us something more about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This happened all in the south, and what I know of this is, as an intelligence man of the company, was that I was placed in the north, and I only read the reports during the morning sessions of the battalion. What I know is that there was a build-up of BSA forces not only patrolling in the last phase before the enclave fell, but also really entering the enclave, and we did not know at that time that the BiH was launching raids outside of the enclave. So what I mean to say is, what we saw were BiH soldiers defending in the last phase, trying to defend the enclave, and trying to get us helping the BiH. But we couldn't help them, because we were, as UN soldiers, had to be impartial. And we saw a strong build-up by the BiH, and rolling up, more or less, our OPs in the southern part of the enclave, starting with OP Echo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, my question related to the period before the build-up of the Serb forces. Did you receive any information prior to that about these attacks which the Army of BH launched from the enclave, after which the ABiH men would go back to the enclave? I'm therefore referring to, say, early June 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. In the transcript, you mentioned the build-up by the BiH. Is that what you said: The build-up by the BiH, the strong build-up by the BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said, from something like the seventh line from the bottom, "And we saw a strong build-up by the BiH and rolling up our OPs in the south of the enclave, starting with OP Echo."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. That isn't not correct. We saw a strong build-up of the BSA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: BSA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And rolling -- and the BSA was starting to rolling up our OPs. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think there is a slight difference between --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I don't think you answered my question.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I think that I answered your question in regard of the build-up. In early June there was no real knowledge to us at that moment that the BiH was launching raids from out of the enclave on the BSA villages around the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, to your knowledge, did anyone else, except your battalion, somebody else from the Dutch army, could acquire such information without being a member of your battalion, or being in one way or another -- having to do with your battalion, being linked to your battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We couldn't go over the boundary of the enclave. We could only see with our binoculars what happened. And we didn't hear about raids, about the BiH throughout the enclave, on Serb villages around the enclave. And I don't know -- at least to me it is not known if there anyone was that had such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you because this is part of the report of the Dutch Ministry of Defence. But let me move on to another question. Captain Rutten, you mentioned humanitarian convoys arriving through the Serb territory. Did you know that weapons had been found in these convoys? Did you ever receive information to that effect, about weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: At the moment the humanitarian convoy came in, the trucks were driven by mostly UN personnel. We escorted the convoys from OP Papa to the warehouse in Srebrenica. At OP Papa I saw several times that the convoys were being checked by the Bosnian Serb army, and the times that I was there, there had never been a weapon found on the UNHCR convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said at the time that you were there. But did you perhaps hear from some other members of Dutch forces that something had been found at some other time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: To my knowledge, and the other soldiers from other patrols that accompanied UNHCR convoys, I never heard that there were weapons found. It could be, but it's not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Captain Rutten, did you know that what we call the Bosnian Muslim army, or the BH army, was being armed by receiving weapons from outside the enclave, and that those weapons were getting into the enclave? Did you receive that kind of information?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, we got some information that there were some routes that came in from the southern part and that the BH army was getting supplies from those routes. And we saw also that there were some new uniforms coming in for the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, are you aware that part of those armaments arrived by helicopter, and have you heard anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There were some reports of our OPs that mentioned that they had seen a helicopter fly over the enclave, but they didn't actually see that the helicopter landed and got unloaded. So no one of the UN personnel, of the battalion, saw really those helicopters unload equipment for the BH army. We saw what I earlier mentioned, that there came some in, but what we saw were mostly uniforms, because they were brand new and, yeah, appeared to us that some materiel was coming in, but not in a large amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask the usher -- Your Honour, I won't test your patience much longer. I only have another fragment from this report. The passages I'm referring to are 4.13 and 4.14.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, I shall read out to you the passage numbered 4.13, and will you please just confirm whether you knew about the event which you described in it. "Soldiers of the army of BH, fully dressed and wearing blue berets or blue caps, arrived within 50 metres from one of the observation posts. Operating as UN personnel, they opened fire from that position in the direction of the VRS front line so it seemed that the UN had opened fire. In this manner they tried to draw the fire of the army of Republika Srpska to the observation post and thus embroil the DutchBat combat in operations." Captain Rutten, did you know about this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting my colleague in his examination, but again I have the English translations of that, and if those could be furnished to the witness, it might assist him in answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That would be very good, thank you, and it would assist the Judges too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps 4.13 and 4.14, which are the excerpts that counsel is referring to could be the only ones shown on the ELMO, since the previous paragraph is not one that has been introduced by my colleague. And I think it would be appropriate, if he wants to introduce it, if we want to introduce it, we make the introduction of that separately. So if the ELMO could only show 4.13 and 4.14, that's the appropriate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Captain Rutten, were you aware of the incident which is described in passage 4.13?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, not this kind of incident. What I see here is -- yeah, there is no location, real location mentioned in the enclave. So, yeah, it's kind of a vague statement, what's standing here. The only thing I can say about our UN equipment was that every time we missed something at our compound, that had gone or whatever, we had an immediate search action that could bring up the last of the uniforms or berets. So this is a very vague statement to me, and you have to give me a location so that we -- so that I can see where it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the Ministry of Defence says only what it says, I mean, using these broad terms, so evidently we shall have to investigate it further. But Captain Rutten, I should like to seize this opportunity, while we have this English translation available to us, to read also passage 4.14. "It also transpired that the BH soldiers were not always recognisable as military personnel. Men who had previously been seen in uniforms fighting in the southern part of the enclave, recognised by members of the DutchBat when they mingled, dressed in civilian clothes with refugees moving from Srebrenica to Potocari, or when they were observed in the Potocari compound. Local women who were known to be members of the ABiH were subsequently also seen in civilian clothes." Captain Rutten, do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I ask that the English translation be provided to the witness so he can review that. That was a rather fast translation, and I'm not sure whether he got it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Let's do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If the item on the ELMO could be placed in front of the Captain, he can read it and then perhaps he could answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Whenever there is an English translation, we'd appreciate having it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I earlier mentioned that I saw a soldier in a wheelbarrow this morning, and it was also a BiH soldier wearing civilian clothes. The same thing I find here now on paper, also that women had been members of the BiH army. Some of them were, really. But in spite of the situation, I would add something. If you know that every BSA soldier looked at the man and makes signs like I made this morning to the throats and had a kind of terror look, and looking through the history, what had earlier happened, about the Bosnian Serb army now facing a problem of leaving the enclave, I myself also would dress up in civilian clothes and leave the army, because what is your chance, really? I would ask the question to you: What is the chance, really, to leave the enclave if you know that you have been shot or will be detained in a house in which you are not being held as a prisoner of war but merely being held up and put on buses and driven out of the enclave? So knowing that, and they also got some intelligence, but knowing that, I would also dress up in civilian clothes and leave the enclave. And what here is on paper, yes, I think that I was in such a situation, I would do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are confirming that this, indeed, happened. Captain Rutten, another thing. You described the place where you found nine bodies. I do not want us to go back to photographs and a map. But could you tell us roughly how far from the place where you found those nine bodies and where Lieutenant Oosterveen also found nine bodies, could you also tell us the distances between those places?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: If I know my way there, and I do, it's more or less 150 metres, maybe some less even, between the places of the bodies. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. I think we can continue. I will ask Judge Wald. Would you like to have a break? I would like to ask the interpreters, who are very valuable to us. Would you like to have a rest, or can we continue? I'll suggest a 20-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You have no questions. Thank you. I would now like to ask my colleague, Judge Wald, if she would like to ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Captain Rutten, in the beginning of your testimony, you talked about the fact that there was a gradual restriction in the number of humanitarian convoys that were allowed into Srebrenica during some of those early months that preceded the attack. My question to you is: Was that decrease raised with the Serbian liaisons, and what if any justification or excuse did they give for adopting a tougher policy on letting the convoys in?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Mostly that information didn't come to us, but what I heard of the battalion was that the Serbs were decreasing the number of convoys by simply not giving them permission to go into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes. But was this raised by your forces, DutchBat forces, or anybody with the Serbs, with a demand for some explanation?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: What I know of is that our negotiation team did discuss that with Major Nikolic and the post next to OP Papa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But you don't know what the reason or the answer that the Serbian liaison people gave?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. When the UN trucks -- when some UN trucks carried some of the refugees from the Srebrenica proper up to Potocari, and we saw earlier film clips of people on those trucks, do you know where they took them? Did they take them right inside the compound or did they leave them on the outskirts of the compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The trucks? The UN trucks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The Dutch trucks drove up to Srebrenica, near the Bravo compound, picked up there the refugees, and they didn't need to pick them up, really, because they more or less stormed the trucks. They got on the trucks, got even inside the trucks, but up the trucks. The driver couldn't even see where he drove. So they were completely filled up. And then they came to Potocari, and they drove into the factory almost to give them the security that we could guarantee them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So they were, to your knowledge, mostly taken at least into the factory compound.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: At another point in your testimony, you said that you -- I think it was maybe the first night, the second night, were told to secure the refugees on the outside of the UN compound in Potocari. What did "secure" mean? Did it mean simply what you told us about, that you got tapes and tried to tape off the area to at least alert the Serbians that that's where the refugees were, or did "secure" mean something different, that you were supposed to patrol it, to try and make sure that they were not molested?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: With "secure" I meant, and I'll give you an estimate of the total situation, in the south of the bus remise were still remains of the B Company that was securing the south side. At the other side, there were the three groups that I earlier mentioned, the three groups of ten men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We patrolled the site that we spoke about. We spoke with the people, we helped them. My team had a doctor, so to give them the first medical aid during the whole night. And more or less we secured them not only by the red/white tape, but just by being there and walking around, and looking up into the hills, that there was no one coming down. And on my side, that night, no one came down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. At another point in your testimony you told us about being actually detained for several hours by the Serb soldiers before you were allowed to go back to the compound, and that was during one of the days when the busing was actually taking place; correct? Now, when you got back from the period of detention, were most of the buses gone by that time, or did the busing continue for a long period after that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The day that you speak about is the 12th, and then during -- in the early evening, the buses stopped coming and there were no buses around anymore. The next day, very early, new buses came and the drivers had to wait for the instructions from the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You also told us that one of the pictures that you took, or you almost took, in this case you didn't take it, you thought would have not portrayed a, I think you said, good scene because it would have looked as though the UN people, the UN soldiers were actively participating in the separation, in the evacuation. Can you tell us a little bit more about what that scene was, and what was the reality? I mean, what was the reality of the UN soldiers taking any active part in the actual separation and evacuation of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I did make some pictures. I did that first because it was difficult because around the APCs there were also the Bosnian Serbs around. The situation was that they had taped an area in which you could place more or less 60 to 70 people, and that was the UN, the Dutch UN personnel that did that. Then they came in, 60 until 70 people. They were more or less shown the way to the buses, or directed to the buses. And between another line there was standing all the people that were waiting, and in spite of the heat, many people were falling down. Dutch soldiers helped them, stood them up, gave them water, helped women with children, to hand out water and to cool them. So that was the situation at the place. And that didn't give a good estimate of the situation, because what I saw through the camera, and actually I made some pictures, was that the Bosnian Serb army was sitting along the road on all kinds of things, with their weapons in front of them, and we were actually at work there, so more or less helping with the deportation. And I found that not a good way to do that, in spite of the things that I heard from my commander and my other colleagues. Because it looked like we were not an impartial party anymore, and as we had our blue caps on, our blue berets on, we had to be an impartial party. So I told that to my colleague, and that was Lieutenant van Duijn, and, okay, he did see that from a different point of view, but I did discuss that with him. But it went on like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Were UN soldiers working with the refugees at the point where the men were being separated from the women?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. At that point, that was at the other side of the line of the buses, and there were some Bosnian Serb soldiers instructing that the men are -- had to be separated from the rest of the family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So there were no UN personnel around that particular operation.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When you visited the White House on the various times, did you ever see any signs in there of violence, torture, in the sense of -- we've heard in other locations of blood, tissue, anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, we couldn't see any. We tried to avoid that more or less by placing some UN soldiers around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You also identified a man with a moustache in one of the Prosecutor's exhibits as somebody who appeared to be, at least at one point in time, in charge, or of a higher echelon, appeared to be engaging with anybody who came in and possibly giving orders. Was that the only person that you had any information, either from your own observation or from hearing, that was in charge of the operations at the White House, of all the men coming in, later on going out in the buses, et cetera? Was he the only one that you could identify during that whole period as having some position of authority as to what went on in the White House?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There were some more people that I identified. For instance, the so-called Captain Mane that I spoke earlier off, he was at the blockade but not actually with the White House itself. I couldn't recognise any specific leader that I've shown here on the photographs or on maps or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Two more questions is all I have. As the buses went off, the early buses that had the women and children on them, and went off to Kladanj, did you later on get any reports back from the other side that those buses had actually gotten to their destination and the women and children had actually crossed over into Muslim territory? So that you knew that at least the women and children were -- those buses were going to where they said they were going?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We had -- some information came in from other colleagues that were brought back, that were on the route escorting some buses. Two days later, some of the -- for instance, Lieutenant Egbers came back, told us about the situation, what had happened there, and also I can refer to our Dutch television, two days later, that we saw actually -- yeah, it's more or less an incident. A woman that we helped, that had something -- a fragment of a grenade in her leg, and she was in a pink training suit. That same woman I saw on television two days later, near Tuzla, and telling that Dutch soldiers had done nothing. So we helped her two days earlier, and she said that nothing had been done. So we knew that the women mostly and the children got to Tuzla airfield. That was more or less two days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But while the evacuation was going on, in the two days when the buses were leaving Potocari, did you at that point know that the women and children were mostly being allowed to go across the border, or were you still in the dark as to what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We were still in the dark, as you called it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question has to do with the two excerpts from the Dutch Ministry debriefing, because I had a little trouble. I think you, in the main, agreed with these, but I had a little trouble understanding how they came together. In one of those, it was said, I believe, although I don't have the English translation here, that sometimes the Muslims inside the enclave, inside the Srebrenica enclave, were helped by the local police. And then the second part of my question is: Later on, in the second excerpt that Mr. Visnjic read, it said that some parts of the VRS were, in fact the soldiers, were supplemented by something called the radical police. What I'm trying to get at is, in your observations in Srebrenica, were the local police allied with one side or the other, and if so which side?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The local police that were still in Srebrenica, in the enclave itself, consisted only of Muslim people. So there must be some ties there because I can't conclude any other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So when the second excerpt talked about the Serb army being supplemented by the radical police, that's something different, in your view?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Wald. Captain Rutten, I also have some questions to ask you, after listening to your very clear testimony. I would like to make sure that I understood the main lines of your testimony. First, in your answer to the Defence counsel, Mr. Visnjic, you told him that the BiH army, you cannot speak of a real army structure. It was refugees collected by Mr. Oric with small arms. Now, I'm going to ask you the same question concerning the Bosnian Serb army. What would you say?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I would say totally different. They were well structured. As I tried to say before to the Defence, in the northern part, there was the Bratunac Brigade, for instance; in the south, the Milici Brigade, all parts of the Drina Corps. We had some information about that, but not all that specific. But you could see during the whole operation that -- and by that I meant the things that I really saw myself -- that everything was well prepared and a well preplanned machinery that you could see from the moment of the arrival, and the time before you could also see that. Everything was well planned, was well overthought. You could see that everything and every man knew exactly what to do. They even had signs at their -- like me, to show that I'm a captain or whatever. Everyone knew who the other was. In fact, that is the perfect way to work with each other and also is a perfect way that your opponent, or an impartial party, can never recognise any of your people at all, because they all told us all kinds of nicknames. So as I refer to this so-called Mr. Mane. Mr. Mane is a well-known nickname with the Serbs. So you see all kinds of things with the structure, and thinking about it, it's almost like, yeah, that it was all well prepared and preplanned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. Well planned. And what about the chain of command or orders, was it, in your assessment as a military man, conformed to the military rules, obeying the superior and orders going down in a chain?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The things that I saw were that the ones that were in command only have to say things once, and everyone understood what he meant or what the senior commander meant. So you could easily tell then who was in control. So it was well-structured, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: According to your testimony, you went through -- I mean, this is really the thrust of your testimony -- you went through two main difficult experiences. The one is concerning the UN, or the DutchBat, the UN representative soldiers, and I noted sometime some of your descriptions, you said that your soldiers were used as shields sometimes. I'll take them in order. Were any of them killed or touched as shields?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not at that moment that I described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But they were used later. They were touched later.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And some were hurt?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. No one got hurt at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But they were used?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: They were used, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The UN soldiers representing the International Community.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And I'm now going gradually. You were laughed at when you always interfered and wanted just to put things in order or to request something, you were just laughed at and ridiculed.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And then going further, you were looted.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's also right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Your jeeps were hijacked.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's also right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And to go further, you sometimes had a pistol at your neck.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, also my neck, my mouth, everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And do you think that was serious, or they were just joking with you? How did you take it then?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I think that it was serious. Walking around for some time and trying to get some information, as I did, they knew exactly who they had to send away, and some of them they couldn't send away easily just by telling them, so they had to be more specific, if I can call it like that, by placing, for instance, a weapon in their face. And it was serious -- it was serious threats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you consider that your life could be in danger --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- if you did your job?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, did you raise the matter to the superiors? And whom did you raise it to?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The moment that our things at the bus remise were looted, sometime afterward, there was a Dutch Captain Melchers who accompanied this so-called Mr. Nikolic. I said that we were not only looted, but also being threatened by the BSA, and he said, "No, we don't do that, and if you all keep quiet, nothing is going to happen." So more or less he said also the same thing as the other soldiers and the other commanders, that, yeah, he ridiculed it, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And after your complaints, the same thing was repeated?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It did not stop?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It did not stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And in other places.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. It did not stop as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you felt that there was a general attitude systematically applied.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was systematically, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In spite of the complaints.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: In spite of the complaints, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, I just wanted to make sure that you were not falling into the hands of some undisciplined soldiers who did not know who you were and whom you represented.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: They knew exactly who I was, they even asked me for my rank, and they knew exactly who was in charge. They could see that. They easily -- they didn't speak to the soldiers. They more or less addressed always the lieutenants that were around. So they knew exactly what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The second line, of course, of your experience was the fate of the Muslims of Srebrenica. You were an eyewitness of nine corpses, nine dead people.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Apparently freshly killed. And you saw in the White House what you called the smell of death, and you saw children of 13 years old. So they reached that age of 13 years old, the children?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: My estimation at that time was 12, 13, some maybe 14, but not all of them. They were also in the house with the older men, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you did not know what was their fate afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Later on I heard, but not at that moment. But seeing the whole structure of it, when you're standing at the fence in front of the house seeing the steps, one after each other, by throwing off their rucksacks, throwing down on the ground their belongings, and as I said earlier, it's no -- it was very clear that there needn't be any identification on the persons. There just was a point where they collected all men together, and at that point they tried to get them on the buses to anywhere, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But on the face of it, they were supposed to be checked to know -- I mean, apparently they went to the White House for inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was the story, but this morning I also told that when you do a proper inquiry, you always leave the ID with the person or you mark envelopes or whatever, just to get a system in it, to recognise who's who in the house. And if you only throw back the stuff on the ground and go into the house, then you never can be sure who's in the house or to interrogate or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it was indiscriminate, in your opinion.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was just because they were men.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I think that just -- that was the main reason, and you could see it at the beginning of the line of the buses, the immediate separation of the soldiers -- of the men by Bosnian Serb soldiers, the dividing of the families almost immediately at the moment that they got walking to the buses, to the White House. That was a well-planned and well -- almost, I would almost say well-rehearsed is the word for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But the women were left out.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Women were left out. Women, very old men, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the children?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: -- and the children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Children under 13.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, and very young children, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, about women, you happen to have seen yourself a woman running, chased by a Serb soldier. Was she running out of her house? Was he dragging her out of her house? What exactly was the scene?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The scene was that the woman ran out, probably out of her house, I don't know really, but she ran out of the house, and shortly after, almost directly, a Serb soldier came after her, in a camouflage uniform, and chased her around the house. And that was what I saw at an instant. And then we had some shots on the spot where we were taking photographs, so I saw nothing more of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That was for looting for rape or for what?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I couldn't make out of that situation what was really happening. Just a woman being chased by a Bosnian Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was that the only case you saw during your stay there, the only case where women were chased?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only case that I saw that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Or heard of?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I heard about some more things, but I can't state them, really, here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Perhaps my last question. Of course, you could not follow at all the buses which were taking the refugees, and at a certain moment they would hijack your jeeps. Did you know afterwards where these buses went and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We were told that all buses were going on the route to Kladanj, but we did never know, because it wasn't a secure route and the men that were on the route of our battalion were held in houses, so we never were really sure what happened with the refugees in the buses because it wasn't a UN-secured road. It was under the surveillance of the Bosnian Serb army. So we had to wait and see who was coming in near Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And was there anything? Later was anything found?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There was -- as we saw later and heard later, there were people coming in finally at Tuzla airbase, and they were all refugees from the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Men or women or old people?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Only women, children, small children, and some very old men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But the other men, nothing in sight?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. There were -- in the first -- one of the first convoys, you can call them like that, there were two Dutch officers with it, and it was Major Boering and a Captain Voerman, and they saw many refugees coming in at Tuzla airbase, and that was only the women, very old men, and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Nothing discovered concerning the men who were taken apart?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, they didn't discover anything because they were also held at the convoy route and then at Tuzla airbase, so they couldn't see anything else, just the bus they were riding with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Captain Rutten. I think this ends our witness, and he can walk out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge Riad, I would move into evidence Prosecutor's Exhibits 82 through 85 and Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/3C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, do you have any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no objections, but I would like to use the opportunity also to tender three exhibits which we have offered, as Defence Exhibits 11, 12, and 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then we'll accept all these exhibits. Thank you. I would like to thank you again, Captain Rutten, for your help to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Whom shall we have now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is Captain Vincentius Egbers. And while we're waiting for Captain Egbers, may I tender into evidence Prosecutor's Exhibit 1/E/1. It is an exhibit which is a smaller version of this map, Prosecutor's 1E, minus the various relevant sites that are attached, and I'm tendering this for purposes of convenience for the Court, if the Court may wish to use this exhibit and counsel may wish to use this exhibit for whatever purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Visnjic, you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. So we'll tender it into evidence. Would you like to call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge Riad, I believe that the usher has gone to collect Captain Egbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, perhaps we can have a break at twenty to two for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Please be seated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to thank you for coming to testify and to contribute to justice being done. Our Prosecutor, Mr. Harmon, will ask you some questions before the Defence counsel will also take over. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Egbers, could you spell your last name for the record?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: E-g-b-e-r-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You are currently serving in the Netherlands Air Force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you have the rank of captain?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: From 1988 to 1998, were you serving in the Royal Dutch Army?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you deploy to Srebrenica with DutchBat III in January of 1995, and did you remain in the enclave of Srebrenica until July the 21st, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges what were your duties and responsibilities within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: In the enclave I was a platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what did you do as a platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: As a platoon commander, I was responsible for a piece of -- the section of our company's terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have placed on the ELMO Prosecutor's Exhibit 89, please. Mr. Usher, I'm particularly interested in having just the area of the Srebrenica enclave appear on the ELMO; the rest is not relevant for the purposes of the testimony, at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Egbers, this is an exhibit that I prepared after talking to you. Can you explain this exhibit to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: You see at the north of the enclave, this was the terrain of the Charlie Company [indicates]; the south of the enclave was the terrain of the Bravo Company, over here [indicates]. My company commander divided his terrain into three sections; the section for the 1st Platoon [indicates], the 2nd Platoon [indicates], and for the 3rd Platoon [indicates], and it was my job to man Observation Post Alpha in the west and to patrol with my platoon in the section of this area. So I was the platoon commander of the 3rd Platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the 3rd Platoon is in the area in which you patrolled with -- the 3rd Platoon is the area marked in yellow on Prosecutor's Exhibit 89?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's marked in yellow. This is the terrain, sir [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say OP Alpha, that's the spot indicated with the letter "A" next to it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the spot marked with "M", was that also in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It was, until the last month of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And is that OP Mike?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: OP Mike was a non-permanent observation post until June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So your principal responsibilities then, Captain Egbers, were in the yellow, pie-shaped area.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In addition, were you also part of a reserve platoon or a reserve unit of the DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Starting in April 1995, we've had a lot of shortage of gasoline, diesel, and we had a big problem with our soldiers who were at leave. The Bosnian Serbs didn't allow them to come back to the enclave. So we were -- my platoon wasn't 30 persons big, but it was a lot smaller. All the platoons had a shortage of men. They were in Zagreb waiting for clearance to come back to the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, a platoon is normally 30 people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what happened? Why was your platoon reduced in size?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, the Bosnian Serbs had to clearance every transport of troops out of the enclave, and of course clearance them back then. And soldiers were allowed to leave the enclave, but from April 1995, they were not allowed to come back to the enclave. So they were waiting at Zagreb for a clearance to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And as a result of the lack of clearance by the Bosnian Serbs, the size of your platoon diminished.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It did, sir, and that's why the officers of the northern part of the Charlie Company were at the main base at Potocari, and the officers had to form with a few soldiers a so-called battalion reserve, four APCs who were under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did those reserve members, including yourself, then deploy to other areas in the Srebrenica enclave in order to fill the gap that was left by the inability to fully man your units?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what was the effect of the dilution, if you will, in the number of your soldiers on the ability of DutchBat to perform its mandate?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It's clear that when you've lost one-third of the platoon, it's very hard to man observation posts and patrol in the area, and so that's why we had a lot of pressure on the men who were still in the enclave. And we had to form this battalion reserve and try to support the Bravo Company, who was in the south of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you able to patrol using your vehicles, or is there some reason why you couldn't do that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: We couldn't patrol with our vehicles because of the lack of fuel. And, for instance, when we had to bring water and food to my soldiers in the west of the enclave, we used some local horses. So we would walk all the way up from Potocari to OP Alpha, which is one day going to OP Alpha and coming back again. So we had some fuel, but we had to keep that in case something happened and the APCs had to drive. So from April, there was a lot of -- we were very short of diesel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you short other supplies also as a result of the actions of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We were very short of food. We only had some rice and some fresh packages left. It was not very good for the morale of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What about medicines?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything about medicines, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the time that you were in the enclave, were you able to make an assessment of the Muslim military forces within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: During the first six months of my stay in the enclave, the Muslim soldiers, whether you can call them soldiers or not, the Muslims didn't carry their weapons openly. Only until OP Echo fell and we had some threatening in the south, the Bosnian Muslims carried their weapons openly, and I saw them carrying some AK-47s and some machine-guns in the south of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when did OP Echo fall?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but it was at the end of June or beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How would you assess the organisation of the Muslim armed forces within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, they were not very well-organised. They were badly dressed. They had no uniforms -- a few uniforms, yes. They had only a few weapons. They had no communications, a bad structure. They told us they had a few brigades, but we only saw refugees. And in the end of the month of June, we saw some weapons but not very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, was there a weapons storage depot at UN Bravo Company, and did that location have Muslim heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to get a little bit ahead of the sequence of events, but did you ever see an artillery piece in your entire stay in the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And without going into details of the circumstances, can you tell us when you saw that artillery piece?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I saw that piece of artillery -- that was the second day when I took up the blocking position in the -- near the Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that during the invasion of the enclave by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It was during the invasion of the south of the enclave that I saw a piece of artillery called a Mike 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that a heavy piece of artillery?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No, it's just a small piece of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges the circumstances, just briefly, about what you know about that particular piece of artillery?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: They had the piece of artillery for a few years in the surrounding of my blocking position, Bravo 1, and they've only had a few shells. I thought they told me about four or five. And there was a commander of this piece of artillery with a few soldiers, and they communicate by writing notes to their bosses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever see that piece of artillery fired?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the time you saw that piece of artillery, were Bosnian Serb army forces advancing into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, as a professional officer, your overall assessment of the military forces of the Muslims within the enclave as you saw them and experienced them.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I think it was badly organised, badly weaponed, a group of refugees who had to be soldiers. No training, no weapons. I didn't think of them as an army as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Turning your attention to the Bosnian Serb forces, can you give me your assessment of the Bosnian Serb forces, as you experienced them and as you saw them in operation?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, I certainly left the enclave in July 1995 with the buses of refugees, and then I saw the military strength of the Bosnian Serb army. They had anti-aircraft missiles, heavy machine-guns, a lot of AK-47s, anti-tank weapons, grenades. They were heavily armed, well-structured. They had communication lines. There were commanders, there were lieutenants who were in charge of a platoon. There was a military structure. That's what I saw of the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see any tanks?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I did, sir. I saw tanks, ambulances. I saw troop transport trucks. They had it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the army, the Bosnian Serb army that you saw, can you give us your assessment of how it appeared to you to function?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, we learned that tanks won't operate by itself, but tanks would mostly go in with four tanks and support each other. But the Bosnian Serb tanks entered the enclave by itself, they raised their barrels and fired like a piece of artillery on the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the various components of the Bosnian Serb army that you saw appear to be functioning in a coordinated fashion?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, it did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Overall, how would you make an assessment then of the Bosnian Serb army, the elements that you saw?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, they were well-trained, they were structured, they were well-armed. They were more like an army to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you believe or are you able to make a comparison of the two?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, I think the Bosnian Serb army was a real army, like we know armies, and the Muslims, they were just refugees who were carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you believe that the armed elements of the Muslims within the Srebrenica enclave posed a credible military threat to the Bosnian Serb army that surrounded the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge Riad, would this be an appropriate time to take a break for ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: If it's good for you, it will be good for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. This is an appropriate time for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher to place Prosecutor's Exhibit 90 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Captain Egbers, I'd like to draw your attention to the 9th of July and ask you if, as part of the unit of DutchBat, you took up a blocking position somewhere in the south of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges, first of all, could you indicate where, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 90, you took up the blocking position? If you mark it with a highlighter, it might be more effective, and use a green highlighter for the purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: You see the road going to the west [indicates], this is the road. It makes two angles of 180 degrees. I was on this angle here, above the "V".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what I'm interested in, Captain Egbers, is first of all can you tell the Judges the circumstances under which you took up that blocking position, what the purpose of the blocking position was?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: The circumstances were the following: We had to take a blocking position so we could be seen by the Bosnian Serb army with our white vehicles, and we had to draw a line, a line that couldn't be passed by the Bosnian Serb army. It was approximately this line [indicates], there was a blocking position on this line. So the Bosnian Serbs knew that we were on that line and they can't cross that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the record is clear, Captain Egbers has indicated a line that appears to be a line that goes from the right-hand side of this exhibit to the left-hand side of the exhibit, and it is the dark line that appears under the word "Srebrenica".

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It is. So these were blocking positions, not as we were taught green, hidden, but now on top of a hill, with white vehicles and blue helmets, so we could be seen by both parties as being a line they couldn't cross. And from this point, I had a good view to the south, because my commander, who was in Srebrenica, on the compound of the Bravo Company, he couldn't see anything in the south of the enclave. His observation post couldn't see a thing, so the blocking positions had to watch the south with their binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At this point in time, the 9th of July, was the invasion of the enclave by the Bosnian Serb army well under way?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the purpose of your blocking position to at least deter the invasion of the enclave beyond the line you've indicated?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It was. We had to search the terrain for any tanks or Bosnian Serb artillery that were there, and we had to report it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long did you remain at that blocking position?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: We stayed there three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you see on the 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I saw a Bosnian Serb tank entering the enclave, firing at Srebrenica, and going back again. And I town called Pusmulici, it's marked yellow here, it's approximately three kilometres away from my blocking position, and with my binoculars I could see Bosnian Serb infantry entering houses, setting them on fire, and stealing stuff out of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you said also that you could see some tanks coming and firing.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I could, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know the direction of their fire?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I could. They fired into the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were there any military targets, as far as you were aware, in the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No, sir. Just refugees and a UN base.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have an opinion then as to the purpose of the firing of the tank rounds into the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I think they wanted to scare the refugees who were in the city of Srebrenica so that they would go north to Potocari and they could enter the town. They were scaring them, and of course they were wounding them, killing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, was it at this particular location where you saw the artillery piece that was the subject of your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, this was the location. Mike 48 from the -- stood and watched south. Just the group of soldiers stood by the piece of artillery, didn't fire it, and was just there in case they had to fire it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many Bosnian Serb soldiers did you see advancing into the enclave from your particular blocking position on the 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, at first I just saw tanks coming into the enclave, firing, and going back again, but at the end of the day I saw infantry entering the enclave as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How were they entering the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: They were coming with a transportation, an ambulance going after them as well, and they were walking one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So walking single file, then?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: You can call it single file, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: They were in green camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell from your location how they were armed?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: They were armed with AK-47s and just rifles, so to me it appeared to be one or two infantry platoons heading for the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You may have mentioned earlier, but what were you making your observations with? What kind of an optical device were you using?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: We had several binoculars, but we had one special one which could go onto 60 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sixty power.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Sixty power, yes, you could call it that way. So we could see very clearly in the south, and that's what we reported. When we reported that the infantry was heading for the town of Srebrenica, we were ordered to accompany the four APCs that were on the marketplace already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you then returned to the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: We did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you see in the town of Srebrenica when you returned?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: When I arrived at the marketplace, I saw thousands of women, children, men. And I saw the men carrying anti-tank weapons. I saw machine-guns and AK-47s. And there was a total chaos at the time because they knew the Bosnian Serbs were entering the town, the south of the town. They were very scared. They were asking me what to do and they were pointing their RPGs on my vehicle. They wanted me to join the other four APCs who were in the south of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "they," are you referring to Muslim men who were armed?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, had you ever seen so many Muslim men with arms prior to this date?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I saw prior to this date a few Muslims carrying weapons openly in the south of the enclave. After OP Echo fell, we had two mobile OPs in the south called Sierra and Uniform, so I saw Muslims carrying openly their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you redeploy to a different location?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I did, sir. I did enter the marketplace and I joined the other four APCs, and then I went back to cover the APCs and stood there all night.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at some point in time, while you were at that location or near that location, were you aware that close air support was being summoned?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: In the early morning, my forward air controller, who was in my APC, had to go back to position Bravo 1 because at 0700 there would be a gunship firing at all the targets, the tanks, artillery, in the south of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what results occurred as a result of any close air support that you received?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
